title: Binary Subarrays with Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every subarray sum directly versus the atMost(goal) - atMost(goal-1) reduction using a variable-size sliding window.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given a binary array nums and an integer goal, return the number of non-empty subarrays whose sum equals exactly goal.

blocks.caption: Count subarrays with sum <= goal, minus those with sum <= goal - 1, to isolate exactly goal

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A binary array nums (values 0 or 1), and an integer goal"],["Output","The count of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly goal"],["Goal","Find this count in a single linear pass (or two), without checking every possible subarray individually"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4; nums[i] is 0 or 1; 0 <= goal <= nums.length"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking for the COUNT of subarrays matching an EXACT sum","Reframe \"exactly goal\" as \"at most goal\" minus \"at most (goal - 1)\""],["All elements are non-negative (here, binary)","A variable-size sliding window works for \"at most\" counting, since the running sum only ever grows as the window grows"],["A fixed target with monotonic sum behavior","The classic atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) counting trick, reusable whenever exact-count problems reduce to a monotonic at-most count"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a binary array nums and an integer goal, count how many contiguous subarrays sum to exactly goal.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Baskets With Exactly N Apples, Via Two Easier Counts
blocks.text: Like wanting to know how many ways exist to pick a contiguous run of baskets containing exactly N total apples, but it's easier to instead count "runs with at most N apples" and "runs with at most N-1 apples" separately, since counting an upper bound with a sliding window is much simpler than counting an exact target directly. The difference between those two easier counts is exactly the answer.

blocks.caption: atMost is easy to count directly with a sliding window; subtracting isolates the exact target

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1,0,1,0,1], goal = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Count of subarrays with sum <= 2: 14. Count of subarrays with sum <= 1: 10","atMost(2) = 14, atMost(1) = 10","Every subarray with sum exactly 2 is counted in atMost(2) but not in atMost(1)"],["Answer","4","14 - 10 = 4: the subarrays [1,0,1], [0,1,0,1], [1,0,1,0], and [1,0,1,0,1] shifted appropriately all sum to exactly 2"]]}

blocks.text: Example: nums = [0,0,0,0,0], goal = 0

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every possible non-empty subarray sums to 0, since all elements are 0","atMost(0) = 15 (all C(5,2)+5 = 15 subarrays), atMost(-1) = 0","Every one of the 15 possible non-empty subarrays of a length-5 array qualifies"],["Answer","15","15 - 0 = 15"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: goal = 0
When goal is 0, atMost(goal - 1) becomes atMost(-1), which is defined as 0 directly (no subarray can have a negative sum), so the answer reduces to simply atMost(0).
5. How Should We Think?
Before checking every possible subarray's sum directly, notice that counting an exact target is harder than counting an upper bound, and the two are related by a simple subtraction.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: All elements of nums are non-negative, so as a window's right boundary grows, its sum can only stay the same or increase, and shrinking from the left can only decrease it. This monotonic behavior is exactly what makes a variable-size sliding window valid for counting "sum <= limit" subarrays.

Observation 2: Counting subarrays with sum EXACTLY equal to goal is significantly harder to do directly with a sliding window, since the window can't just grow or shrink monotonically toward an exact target.

Observation 3: However, "exactly goal" is precisely "at most goal" minus "at most (goal - 1)", and "at most" is straightforward to count: for every right endpoint, once the window's sum exceeds the limit, shrink from the left until it doesn't; every subarray ending at that right endpoint, starting anywhere from the current left to right, has sum at most the limit, contributing (right - left + 1) to the count.

Observation 4: Compute atMost(goal) and atMost(goal - 1) using this technique, and subtract.

Recognizing the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction is a broadly reusable trick whenever an "exactly k" counting problem can be reduced to a monotonic "at most k" one.
This is the classic "at most k" counting sliding window pattern, applied twice and subtracted, to isolate an exact-count target.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible starting index, extend forward one element at a time, checking whether the running sum equals goal exactly.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, accumulating a running sum.
Whenever the running sum equals goal exactly, increment the count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh running sum is used for every starting position, since each independent walk accumulates its own subarray sum.
The sum is never reset mid-walk, since every extension naturally builds on the previous partial sum.
count increments every time the running sum happens to equal goal exactly, regardless of whether it exceeded goal before or after.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible subarray is checked directly via its running sum, so the correct count is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n starting positions walks forward up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: checking every (start, end) pair directly ignores that "at most" counting with a monotonic sum admits a linear-time sliding window solution, and that the exact-count target can be derived from two such at-most counts.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every subarray's exact sum directly. Instead, define atMost(limit) as the count of subarrays with sum <= limit, computed via a single sliding window pass (since all elements are non-negative, the window's sum only ever grows as it grows and shrinks as it shrinks, making the "shrink until valid" logic always correct). Then, since "exactly goal" is "at most goal" minus "at most (goal - 1)", compute atMost(goal) and atMost(goal - 1) and subtract.

Implement atMost(limit) as a standard variable-size sliding window: grow the window by advancing right, adding to a running sum; whenever the sum exceeds limit, shrink from the left. For every right endpoint, add (right - left + 1) to the running subarray count, since every subarray from left to right (inclusive) up to this right endpoint has sum at most limit. The final answer is atMost(goal) - atMost(goal - 1).
9. Optimized Solution
Compute atMost(goal) and atMost(goal - 1) using a variable-size sliding window each, then subtract.
Dry run for nums = [1,0,1,0,1], goal = 2: computing atMost(2)
Dry run for nums = [1,0,1,0,1], goal - 1 = 1: computing atMost(1)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: atMost(2) - atMost(1) = 14 - 10 = 4, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since each atMost call runs a single linear sliding window pass, and there are only 2 such calls.
Space: O(1) extra.
Why This Works

Because every element is non-negative, a window's sum only ever increases as it grows and decreases as it shrinks, guaranteeing that "shrink until sum <= limit" always finds the correct, unique boundary. For each right endpoint, every subarray from some left' (left <= left' <= right) to right has sum at most limit, contributing exactly (right - left + 1) new valid subarrays. Subtracting atMost(goal - 1) from atMost(goal) removes every subarray with sum strictly less than goal, leaving only those with sum exactly goal.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: atMost is a self-contained helper reused for both the goal and goal - 1 calls, keeping the logic in one place.
The negative-limit guard (limit < 0 returns 0) handles the goal = 0 edge case cleanly without a separate branch elsewhere.
subarrays accumulates (right - left + 1) at every step, which is the count of new valid subarrays ending exactly at this right endpoint.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction is a broadly reusable technique whenever "exactly k" is hard to count directly with a sliding window, but "at most k" is straightforward due to monotonic (non-negative) sum behavior.
Common mistakes

items: Trying to slide a window directly toward an exact sum target, which doesn't work cleanly since growing or shrinking the window can both overshoot and undershoot an exact value.
Forgetting the goal = 0 edge case, where atMost(goal - 1) = atMost(-1) must be explicitly handled as 0, not computed by the general sliding window logic.
Adding just 1 instead of (right - left + 1) when counting valid subarrays for a given right endpoint, which undercounts by ignoring all the shorter valid subarrays ending at the same point.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["goal = 0","Counts only subarrays made entirely of zeros"],["goal = nums.length","At most one subarray (the entire array, if it's all ones) can qualify"],["nums is all zeros and goal = 0","Every possible non-empty subarray counts, giving n*(n+1)/2 total"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) reduction explicitly before coding, since it's the crucial insight that turns an awkward exact-sum count into two easy monotonic counts.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count subarrays with sum EXACTLY equal to some target, over non-negative elements" points toward computing atMost(target) - atMost(target - 1), each via a straightforward variable-size sliding window.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this work if nums could contain negative numbers? The monotonic sliding window for atMost breaks down entirely with negatives; a prefix-sum-plus-hashmap approach would be needed instead.
How would you count subarrays with sum in a RANGE [lo, hi] instead of exactly one value? Compute atMost(hi) - atMost(lo - 1) directly, generalizing the same technique.

Could this be solved with a single pass instead of two atMost calls? Yes, using a prefix-sum-count hashmap (tracking how many prefixes have each running sum), similar to Subarray Sum Equals K, though the sliding window version here is simpler to reason about for a binary array.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) technique, reusable for any "exact count" problem over non-negative elements that reduces to a monotonic "at most" sliding window, similar in spirit to how Subarrays with K Different Integers counts exact distinct-value targets.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (atMost(goal) - atMost(goal-1)): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) exact-count reduction, using a variable-size sliding window for each "at most" count
Core Idea: Counting subarrays with sum exactly goal equals counting those with sum at most goal, minus those with sum at most (goal - 1)
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Non-negative elements make "at most" sums monotonic and sliding-window-friendly, even though "exactly" sums are not
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: atMost(goal) minus atMost(goal - 1) equals exactly goal
